preamble: Spirantization of the voiceless bilabial plosive [p] to the voiceless bilabial fricative [ɸ] keeps the place of articulation but releases the closure into friction. It is the usual first step in the weakening chain p > ɸ > h > ∅: Japanese word-initial /p/ became [ɸ] (still heard in fu [ɸɯ]) before most instances went on to [h]; Proto-Celtic turned Indo-European *p into *ɸ before losing it; and in Venda (Bantu) Proto-Bantu *p surfaces as the bilabial fricative written fh. In Cuzco Quechua, /p/ is realized [ɸ] in the syllable coda (/ˈʎiptʼa/ [ˈʎiɸtʼa]).

examples.note: Comparative Ryukyuan evidence and Ainu loans point to an earlier stop *p; word-initial p had become [ɸ] by Early Middle Japanese, rendered as f in 16th-century Portuguese works. Before u the [ɸ] survives in Modern Japanese; scholars disagree on whether the lenition had already happened within the Old Japanese period.
Before other vowels the fricative later went on to [h] (palatal [ç] before i).
The fricative stage is reconstructed rather than attested: *ɸ was lost in all daughter languages, giving Old Irish athair and Gaulish atir.
Venda fh is the voiceless bilabial fricative [ɸ], contrasting with labiodental f.
The locative class 16 prefix shows the same *p > ɸ reflex.
Syllable-coda allophone: Cuzco /p k q/ become fricatives in the coda (Rodríguez Champi 2006).
